intro: Twenty three verses, said in the synagogue on Wednesday morning as the psalm of the day, and the hardest of the daily psalms to say lightly: it opens by asking God to take vengeance and spends its first half on a society where killing the powerless has become normal practice. The turn comes at verse 12, from what God should do to what the sufferer can learn. The grammar to watch is one prefixed letter, the interrogative he-, which is all that separates a statement from the question that carries verses 9 and 10.

stichs.en: God of retribution, LORD,
God of retribution, shine forth.

verses.summary: The psalm opens with the title it needs, repeats it, and then asks for one thing only: appear. What is wanted is visibility, not yet action.

stichs.en: Rise up, Judge of the earth;
pay the proud back what they have earned.

verses.summary: The address changes from God of retribution to Judge of the earth, the same office named by its function. What is asked is payment of a debt, not destruction.

stichs.en: How long shall the wicked, LORD,
how long shall the wicked exult?

verses.summary: The complaint proper begins, and it is about time rather than power. The question is not whether the wicked will fall but how long the delay is allowed to run.

stichs.en: They gush, they speak insolence;
all the workers of iniquity swagger.

verses.summary: Three verbs about the mouth before a single verb about the hand. What marks the wicked first is the noise they make and how safe they feel making it.

stichs.en: They crush Your people, LORD,
and afflict Your inheritance.

verses.summary: The victims are named as God's own, twice, with the possessive suffix carrying the whole argument. The complaint shifts from what the wicked deserve to what God stands to lose.

stichs.en: They kill the widow and the resident stranger,
and murder the fatherless.

verses.summary: The widow, the stranger and the orphan are the three the Torah protects by name. Listing them turns a complaint about violence into a charge that the law itself has collapsed.

stichs.en: And they say: the LORD does not see,
the God of Jacob pays no attention.

verses.summary: The wicked are given one line of direct speech, and it is not a denial that God exists. They grant the existence and deny only the attention, which is the more practical heresy.

stichs.en: Understand, you brutes among the people;
you fools, when will you gain sense?

verses.summary: The psalm stops addressing God and turns on the fools directly. The insult is precise: not wicked here but brutish, unable to reason from what is in front of them.

stichs.en: He who planted the ear, shall He not hear?
He who formed the eye, shall He not look?

verses.summary: The argument from the maker to the faculty, which needs no revelation to work. Whoever installed hearing and sight is not the one thing in the world lacking them.

stichs.en: He who disciplines nations, shall He not rebuke,
He who teaches a human being knowledge?

verses.summary: The same argument extended from the senses to judgement. Whoever disciplines whole nations and gives a person knowledge is not going to run short of either.

stichs.en: The LORD knows the thoughts of a human being,
that they are a breath.

verses.summary: The answer to verse 7 lands. God does know human thinking, and the verdict on it is the lightest word available: vapour, a breath, nothing that holds.

stichs.en: Happy is the man You discipline, LORD,
and whom You teach out of Your Torah,

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. The two verbs of verse 10, disciplining and teaching, come back aimed at one person, and the person is called happy for receiving them.

stichs.en: to give him quiet from the days of evil,
until a pit is dug for the wicked.

verses.summary: The purpose of the discipline is steadiness, not merit. It carries the sufferer through the interval while the end of the wicked is still being prepared.

stichs.en: For the LORD will not abandon His people,
and He will not forsake His inheritance.

verses.summary: The ground of the quiet, stated as a fact about God rather than about the situation. The pair of nouns from verse 5 returns, this time as what cannot be lost.

stichs.en: For judgement will come back to righteousness,
and after it all the upright in heart.

verses.summary: Judgement is described as returning to righteousness, which assumes it has drifted away from it. The exact sense of the line is contested and the second half depends on how you take the first.

stichs.en: Who will rise for me against evildoers?
Who will take a stand for me against the workers of iniquity?

verses.summary: Back into the present tense of the trouble. Both questions expect the answer nobody, which is what makes the next verse work.

stichs.en: If the LORD had not been a help to me,
my soul would soon have settled in silence.

verses.summary: The answer to who will stand up for me. Without that help the speaker would already be somewhere the psalm names only as silence.

stichs.en: When I said, my foot is slipping,
Your kindness, LORD, held me up.

verses.summary: The general claim narrows to one moment. The verb is not rescue from death but a hand under someone already losing their footing.

stichs.en: When my anxious thoughts crowd inside me,
Your consolations delight my soul.

verses.summary: The one verse about the inside of a head. Anxious thoughts multiply, and what answers them is described as delight rather than as a counter-argument.

stichs.en: Can a throne of ruin be allied with You,
one that frames trouble by statute?

glosses: can it be joined to You
verses.summary: The sharpest political line in the book. The question is whether a regime that manufactures harm through legislation can claim any partnership with God.

stichs.en: They band together against the life of the righteous,
and condemn innocent blood.

verses.summary: How that regime works, stated plainly: a coalition against one life, and a verdict returned against blood that everyone knows is innocent.

stichs.en: The LORD has become my high stronghold,
and my God the rock of my refuge.

verses.summary: The answer to verse 16 completed. What rose up for the speaker was not a person but a place to stand, named twice in the vocabulary of high rock.

stichs.en: He turns their own iniquity back upon them,
and by their own evil He will destroy them;
the LORD our God will destroy them.

verses.summary: The end delivers the recompense asked for in verse 2, and imports nothing to do it. The wicked are destroyed by their own work, simply no longer carried away for them.

pardes.body: Four movements. Verses 1 to 7 are the complaint, and they end by quoting the wicked. Verses 8 to 11 answer that quotation with an argument anyone can follow, built on the interrogative he- of {{9.0}} and {{10.0}}: whoever made the ear is not deaf. Verses 12 to 15 turn from what the wicked deserve to what the sufferer receives, and 16 to 23 drop into the first person and testify. The pivot on the word for discipline is deliberate: it disciplines nations in verse 10 and one man in verse 12, and the psalm treats those as the same act at two scales.

Three places repay a second look. {{11.6}} is the word Ecclesiastes uses for everything, breath or vapour, and here it is the verdict on human calculation rather than on human life. {{17.6}} means silence, and is widely read as a name for the realm of the dead rather than a state of quiet, which makes the verse a report of a near miss. {{20.6}} is the ordinary word for a statute or a decree, and the line is not about lawlessness but about harm produced lawfully, which is why it has been so heavily used since. Verse 15 is genuinely unsettled: the syntax allows judgement returning to righteousness or righteousness being the point judgement returns to, and translations divide.

Verse 12 is the seat of the rabbinic category of chastisements of love, suffering read as instruction rather than punishment, and whether such a category exists at all is an old and unresolved argument in the tradition. The tradition that assigns this psalm to the fourth day of the week connects it to the sun and moon made on that day and to a future reckoning with those who worship them, which is why a psalm about human courts is said on a day of luminaries. Verse 9 became a standard argument in its own right: the maker of a faculty cannot be supposed to lack it, and the same reasoning gets applied well beyond the ear and the eye.

The psalm sets two thrones against each other. {{20.1}} is a seat of ruin claiming alliance with God, and verse 22 answers it with a stronghold and a rock, which in the mystical reading are the same image seen from below: the throne one cannot join and the rock one can stand on. The closing verb of {{23.5}} and {{23.6}} is written twice in the Masoretic text, and the repetition is usually read as emphasis rather than error, the pattern of measure for measure stated once for the act and once for the actor. Nothing is added to the wicked in that ending; what they built is simply left with them, which is the strictest form the tradition gives to justice.
